source.title: SAE regularization produces more interpretable models

record.file_problem: Whole post text is present; the referenced charts are not included in the supplied text.
record.tranche_reason: Evaluates SAE reconstruction on a character-based GPT-2 toy model, reporting results relevant to whether SAEs can recover sparse representations; it does not test superposition geometry or its causes.
record.gate_note: The study reports SAE reconstruction metrics, but not whether the SAE latents correspond to complete, stable, or canonical model features. Base-model cross-entropy is also reported, but is not a result about the claim versions. No cited results are treated as study findings.
record.test_reason: The post proposes a training method: SAE-loss regularization during model training. It reports only whether that method improves SAE reconstruction at fixed L0, compared with unregularized training, in a 4-layer character-level GPT-2. It does not test whether superposition exists, its geometry or causes, or whether SAE features are canonical units. The rows compare the study's own method against a baseline, so this is T4.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also claim that regularization did not hurt, and slightly lowered, base-model cross-entropy, possibly deterring overfitting. They note it is computationally costly and unlikely to become popular except for maximally interpretable models. The introduction's 'improves on all layers' is qualified in the results by layer 3's unreliability.
record.recipe_differences: Simultaneously trains SAE layers and model weights using SAE losses as a regularization term; it does not use the original superposition experiment’s method.
record.method_sensitivity: Improvements are less dependable on layer 3. The authors say regularization coefficients that are too large affect model performance; they did not study smaller coefficients.

fits_no_version.finding: In a 4-layer character-level GPT-2, adding SAE losses as a training regularizer gives lower cross-entropy loss increase at fixed L0 for freshly trained SAEs on most layers. Layer 3 is less reliable, and base-model loss is not harmed.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Training-time SAE regularization can make a model's activations more decomposable by SAEs at a given sparsity, without hurting model loss.

record.problems: The experiment uses a small toy model trained on a limited Shakespeare dataset that the authors say easily overfits. Numerical chart values are absent from the supplied text; results are reported qualitatively. The authors did not optimize training parameters or study smaller regularization coefficients, and do not establish generalization to larger models.
record.rows_left_out: No separately reported base-model cross-entropy result was retained because it measures model training loss, not an outcome named by the claim versions.

untested.parts: Not tested: no toy-model geometry, no sparsity transition, no orthogonality analysis.
Not tested: no analysis of capacity or feature importance.
Not tested: no alternative causes of polysemanticity.
Not tested: no LLM, no measure of feature spread across neurons. SAE reconstruction quality is reported only as a regularized-versus-unregularized comparison in a 4-layer, width-64 toy model.
Not tested: completeness, stability and canonicity of SAE features are not examined. The authors note that better SAE metrics need not mean better interpretability.
Not tested: the dimensionality of features is not examined.

record.verdict_notes: This is a methods post on LessWrong, not peer reviewed. All results are qualitative in the text because the charts are missing, and no uncertainty is reported. The reader's limits_scope label on V4 is removed: the rows measure the study's own intervention, not whether models naturally contain SAE-recoverable features.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test overlapping, nearly orthogonal feature directions, a sparsity-dependent transition, or regular geometry.
Does not test whether feature importance and limited capacity cause polysemanticity or dedicated dimensions.
Does not test alternative causes of polysemanticity.
Tests SAE reconstruction on a toy character-based GPT-2, not LLMs; does not test feature spread across neurons or independently verify that recovered latents are underlying model features.
Does not test whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units; the post notes that better SAE metrics do not necessarily imply greater interpretability.
Does not test whether features are one-dimensional directions rather than multidimensional.

rows.subject: character-based GPT-2

conditions.value: Most layers; layer 3 reported separately below
Average across parameter sweeps for ten independently-trained pairs

rows.measure: Cross-entropy loss increase from substituting model activations with SAE-reconstructed activations, at a fixed SAE sparsity level.
rows.baseline: SAE features extracted from weights trained without SAE regularization
rows.value: SAE regularization reliably yields better results on most layers.
rows.note: The post describes the chart’s overall result, but the chart and its numerical values are absent from the supplied text.
rows.check: Compares the study's own method (SAE-regularized training) with unregularized training. This is method performance, not evidence on V4. V4 concerns real LLMs spreading features or containing SAE-recoverable features, and this is a toy model shaped by training toward SAE-friendliness. No numbers are given; the charts are absent.
